## Problem Statement

The internal support export currently retains transcripts for 7 days. Investigations need access to more historical transcript data than that window allows. The approved security policy permits retention up to 30 days, but the current implementation does not use the full allowance.

## Requirements

- The system shall retain internal support export transcripts for a duration greater than 7 days and no more than 30 days, per the approved security policy.
- The existing purge implementation and deployment process shall remain unchanged; only the numeric retention value passed to the existing scheduled purge shall change.

**Assumed**: the scheduled purge job already accepts a numeric retention parameter and requires no code changes to accept a new value, because the user stated it "already works, is tested, and takes a numeric retention value." Correct if wrong.

## Constraints

- Retention duration must not exceed 30 days — hard cap set by the approved security policy, non-negotiable.
- No new or changed interfaces.
- No changes to the deployment process.
- Must reuse the existing scheduled purge job; only its numeric retention-value input changes.

## Success Criteria

- New retention value in effect, greater than 7 days and no more than 30 days.
- Purge behavior verified correct against the new value using the existing (already-tested) purge test suite.
- No interface or deployment changes introduced.
- _[open]_ — exact numeric target retention value, pending stakeholder input.

## Validation Contract

### Acceptance Tests

- Existing purge test suite re-run parameterized against the new retention value; confirms exports older than the new threshold are purged and newer ones retained.

### Regression Checks

- Existing purge test suite passes with the new parameterized value.
- Confirm no export data is retained beyond the 30-day policy ceiling under any configuration drift.

### Failure Signals

- Purge job errors or misbehaves on the new numeric input.
- Any audit finds export data older than the configured retention threshold or beyond the 30-day cap.

### Verification Methods

- Automated: re-run existing parameterized purge test suite against the new value.
- Observational: periodic audit sampling of stored exports' ages post-rollout.

### Feedback Loop Design

- Cheapest fault-localizing signal: run the existing parameterized purge test with the new numeric value before rollout (fast, localizes to the config/purge interaction).
- Cadence: on the config change itself, before deploy.
- Fallback if no fast signal exists: manual sampling of a handful of exports' ages at deploy time.
- Escalation trigger: any test failure, or any export found beyond the configured/policy threshold, widens the check to a full audit of stored exports.

### Known Blind Spots

- Not yet confirmed whether the existing purge test suite genuinely parametrizes the retention value or is hardcoded to 7 days (flagged under Regression Protection, Fragile).

## Inputs

- Current retention configuration (7 days).
- Approved security policy (30-day cap), per user summary.
- Existing scheduled purge job, which accepts a numeric retention value.

## Outputs

- Updated retention configuration value.
- Purge implementation and deployment process, unchanged.

## Out of Scope

- Any change to purge implementation logic.
- Any change to deployment process.
- Any new or modified export/retrieval interface.

## Authority Boundaries

### Executor May Decide

- Where the numeric retention value is stored/configured (implementation detail), as long as it flows into the existing purge job unchanged.
- Exact mechanics of re-running the existing test suite against the new value.

### Executor Must Escalate

- Any indication the target value needs to exceed the 30-day policy cap.
- Any discovery that the existing purge test suite does not actually parametrize retention (i.e., is hardcoded).

### Executor Must Not Change

- Purge implementation logic.
- Deployment process.
- The retention ceiling semantics (must remain ≤30 days per policy).

## Current Interpretation

Increase the internal support export's retention window from 7 days to some value greater than 7 and no more than 30 days, by reconfiguring the numeric retention parameter already accepted by the existing, tested, scheduled purge job — without altering the purge implementation or deployment process. The specific target value and the investigation need it's meant to satisfy are not yet defined.

## Misclassification Risks

### Potential False Positives

- Bumping retention to a trivially "longer" value (e.g., 8 days) would technically satisfy "retain longer" while not actually resolving the investigations' need for more history — appearing done while missing the actual point.

### Potential False Negatives

- Missing confirmation that the existing purge test suite is truly parameterized on retention value rather than hardcoded to 7 days, which would make the "already tested" claim not transfer to the new value.
- Missing stakeholder sign-off tying the new numeric value to an actual investigation lookback requirement, rather than an arbitrary number under the cap.

## Ambiguities

### Blocking

- Exact target retention value (>7, ≤30 days) and the investigation-need/stakeholder rationale behind it. This single gap is the root cause of the sub-70% scores on Clarity, Success, Stakeholders, Risk, and Execution Readiness.

### Non-Blocking

_[open]_

### Intentional

- Interface changes and deployment-process changes are intentionally excluded from scope, per explicit user instruction.

## Risks

- Chosen value may be too low to actually satisfy investigation needs (repeats the current problem at a different threshold).
- Chosen value may sit near the 30-day cap with no margin, risking future policy violation if requirements shift.
- Existing purge tests may not truly be parameterized, risking a silent regression when the config value changes.

## Stakeholders

- Investigations/support team — beneficiary, needs sufficient transcript lookback.
- Security/compliance policy owner — sets and enforces the 30-day cap; likely decision-maker on the final value.
- Support engineering team — implements the config change.
- Whoever originated the "retain longer" request — source of the actual retention target; not yet identified.

responses.reply:
Got it — 14 days, authorized by you as the policy owner, with a concrete pass/fail test (13-day-old transcript retained, 15-day-old purged via the existing suite). That closes the last blocking ambiguity and resolves the five commandments that were sitting below 70% for the same root cause.

Everything else — problem statement, scope (purge implementation and deployment untouched), constraints (30-day cap), and out-of-scope items — carries forward unchanged. All commandments are now stable or explicitly-accepted-fragile, and there's nothing left in Ambiguities → Blocking, so the spec is frozen as Validated (v1) and I've laid out the layered reasoning chain below.

Moving into plan mode now to build the execution plan against this spec.

- Retention duration must not exceed 30 days — hard cap set by the approved security policy, non-negotiable.

- Existing purge test suite passes with the new parameterized value (14 days).
- Confirm no export data is retained beyond the 30-day policy ceiling under any configuration drift.

### Failure Signals

- Purge job errors, or misbehaves, on the 14-day input.
- Test shows a 15-day-old export retained, or a 13-day-old export purged.
- Any audit finds export data older than 14 days (or beyond the 30-day cap) unexpectedly present.

### Verification Methods

- Automated: re-run existing parameterized purge test suite against the 14-day value, checking the 13-day-retained / 15-day-purged boundary.
- Observational: periodic audit sampling of stored exports' ages post-rollout.

### Feedback Loop Design

- Cheapest fault-localizing signal: run the existing parameterized purge test with 14 days as input before rollout (fast, localizes directly to the config/purge interaction).
- Cadence: on the config change itself, before deploy.
- Fallback if no fast signal exists: manual sampling of a handful of exports' ages at deploy time.

### Known Blind Spots

- Not yet mechanically confirmed whether the existing purge test suite genuinely parametrizes the retention value versus being hardcoded to 7 days (carried from Pass 1's Regression Protection/Robustness scoring). ## Inputs

- Approved security policy (30-day cap), per user summary, user acting as policy owner.
- Existing scheduled purge job, which accepts a numeric retention value.

## Outputs

- Purge implementation and deployment process, unchanged.

## Out of Scope

- Any change to purge implementation logic.
- Any change to deployment process.
- Any new or modified export/retrieval interface.

## Authority Boundaries

### Executor May Decide

### Executor Must Escalate

### Executor Must Not Change

- Purge implementation logic.
- Deployment process.
- The retention ceiling semantics (must remain ≤30 days per policy).
- The authorized target value (14 days) without new policy-owner sign-off.

## Current Interpretation

Increase the internal support export's retention window from 7 days to 14 days, by reconfiguring the numeric retention parameter already accepted by the existing, tested, scheduled purge job — without altering the purge implementation or deployment process. The 14-day value is authorized directly by the user acting as the security/compliance policy owner, within the approved 30-day cap. Success is defined concretely: a 13-day-old transcript remains present, and a 15-day-old transcript is purged, verified via the existing purge test suite.

## Misclassification Risks

### Potential False Positives

- None currently outstanding at the "retain longer" ambiguity level — the target is now numerically concrete and owner-authorized, closing the prior risk of a trivially-longer-but-inadequate value.

### Potential False Negatives

- If the existing purge test suite turns out to be hardcoded to 7 days rather than genuinely parameterized, re-running it "as-is" would not actually validate the 14-day behavior — this is flagged as a Known Blind Spot and an escalation condition, not silently assumed away.

## Ambiguities

### Blocking

_None — the prior blocking ambiguity (target retention value) was resolved this pass: 14 days, authorized by the policy owner, with a concrete success test._

### Non-Blocking

- Exact day-14 boundary semantics (inclusive/exclusive) — mechanical test-writing detail, doesn't block planning or execution.
- Whether the existing purge test suite is genuinely parameterized vs. hardcoded — carried as a Known Blind Spot with an explicit escalation path if it turns out hardcoded.

### Intentional

- Interface changes and deployment-process changes are intentionally excluded from scope, per explicit user instruction.

## Risks

- Existing purge tests may not truly be parameterized, risking a silent gap between "tests pass" and "14-day behavior is actually verified" (mitigated by an explicit escalation condition).
- 14 days may, in the future, prove insufficient for longer-running investigations — an accepted, owner-authorized tradeoff rather than an open question at this time.

## Stakeholders

- Investigations/support team — beneficiary, gains a longer transcript lookback window.
- Security/compliance policy owner — the user, who set the 30-day cap and directly authorized the 14-day target this pass.
- Support engineering team — implements the config change.

## Layered Reasoning Chain

```
Layer 1 — Problem
  Investigations lack sufficient transcript history because internal support exports are purged after only 7 days, well short of the 30-day ceiling the security policy already permits.

Layer 2 — Requirements
  The system shall retain internal support export transcripts for 14 days (replacing the current 7-day window).
  The system shall leave the existing purge implementation and deployment process unchanged, changing only the numeric retention value fed into the existing scheduled purge job.
  Challenged by: if 14 days later proves insufficient for an actual investigation, or if the purge job's numeric parameter isn't as decoupled from its implementation as assumed.

Layer 3 — Constraints
  Retention must not exceed 30 days (approved security policy, hard cap).
  No new/changed interfaces; no changes to the deployment process; must reuse the existing scheduled purge job as-is.

Layer 4 — Risks
  The existing purge test suite may not genuinely parametrize retention (could be hardcoded to 7 days), which would mean "already tested" doesn't transfer to the new value.
  14 days is a policy-owner judgment call, not independently derived from a specific investigation case — accepted as a legitimate tradeoff, not a defect.

Layer 5 — Success
  A transcript 13 days old remains present; a transcript 15 days old has been purged; retention config reads 14 days; no interface or deployment changes were introduced.
  False positive guard: a "longer" value that isn't actually 14 days, or that technically increases retention without passing the 13/15-day boundary test, does not count as success.
  False negative guard: an audit finding data retained beyond 30 days, or the purge suite silently not exercising the new value, would mean the result is incomplete even if surface checks pass.

Layer 6 — Validation
  Acceptance tests: existing purge test suite re-run with retention=14, checking the 13-day-retained / 15-day-purged boundary.
  Regression checks: existing suite continues to pass; periodic audit confirms no export exceeds 30 days.
  Failure signals: test failure on the new boundary; any export found older than 14 days (or 30-day cap) in production.
  Verification method: automated (test suite) plus observational (periodic age-sampling audit).
  Feedback Loop Design: run the parameterized purge test with retention=14 before deploy (cheap, fault-localizing); fallback is manual sampling of export ages at deploy time; any failure escalates to a full stored-export audit.

Layer 7 — Execution Readiness
  Inputs: current 7-day config, 14-day authorized target, existing scheduled purge job accepting a numeric parameter.
  Outputs: updated retention config (14 days); purge implementation and deployment process unchanged.
  Authority boundaries: executor may choose where the value is configured and how the existing suite is re-run; must escalate if the target would exceed 30 days or if the suite turns out not to be parameterized; must not alter purge logic, deployment process, or the authorized 14-day value without new policy-owner sign-off.
  Dependencies: none beyond the existing purge job and its test suite.
  Escalation conditions: suite proves hardcoded; any post-rollout audit finds data outside the 14-day/30-day bounds.
```
